chunks.title: anti-dive-anti-squat — Anti-dive and anti-squat (side-view geometry)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `under_lower_arm_shims_ff`, `under_lower_arm_shims_fr`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rf`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rr`
**Concepts:** [[load-transfer]], [[bite-hold]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** The **split** between the forward and rearward inner pickups on an axle (FF−FR front, RF−RR
rear) tilts the lower arm's **inner hinge line in side view**, setting a **pitch centre** — the fore-aft
twin of the [[roll-center]]. It decides how much **longitudinal** load (bra

chunks.title: arb — Anti-roll bar (ARB / sway bar)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `arb_front`, `arb_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-stiffness]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** An ARB is a **bar linking the left and right wheels** at one end of the car. It only
twists when the two wheels move **differently** — that is, in **roll** — so a stiffer bar resists roll
more at that end. When both wheels move **together** (**heave** — a crest, or a bump under both) the bar
just swings and does nothing. So it changes that end's share of roll stiffness withou

chunks.title: awesomatix-spring-gap-damper — Spring gap (Awesomatix effective rate)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `spring_gap_front`, `spring_gap_rear` — Awesomatix-specific stiffness control. **Bigger gap = stiffer** (founder-confirmed). It is an **effective spring-rate adjustment**, not a preload or free-play setting.

Because spring gap is a rate control, **all spring-rate reasoning applies**: read the mechanisms from
[[spring-rate]] and its linked concepts — stiffer at an end means less roll there, load arriving
faster, and a bigger share of that end's lateral load tran

chunks.title: awesomatix-spring-gap-damper — Spring rate is an output of spring gap (Awesomatix)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `front_spring_rate_gf_mm`, `rear_spring_rate_gf_mm` — derived values, not adjusters.

The gf/mm figure is a lookup, not a knob: fitted spring (`std`/`s`) × SRS arrangement (I/II) ×
**effective gap** (`spring_gap` − `lower_arm_extension`), in 0.2 mm steps. There is no continuous
rate adjuster and no intermediate spring to fit, so with the same spring and SRS **a fixed gap is a
fixed rate** — the two cannot move independently, and a given rate is only reachable a

chunks.title: awesomatix-spring-gap-damper — Damper percent (Awesomatix damping / pack)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `damper_percent_front`, `damper_percent_rear` — the Awesomatix damping setting; behaves like **piston size** on a conventional damper. **Higher percent = more damping** (founder-confirmed).

The piston-size character carries a second variable beyond simple more/less: **pack** — resistance that rises **progressively with shaft speed**, so gentle inputs meet similar force while fast movements (bumps, kerb strikes) meet sharply rising force. For the **low-speed** cha

chunks.title: bodyshell-aero — Bodyshell (aero)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `rear_hrb_setting`, `body_position_from_windshield`
**Concepts:** [[aero-load]]

**Physics.** The shell is the car's **main aero device**. Raising its rear, or moving it fore/aft, changes
**how much aero load the body makes and where it acts** — all scaling with **speed²** ([[aero-load]]).
Body **choice** (shell model) is a large aero decision of its own.

chunks.title: bump-steer-toe-gain — Bump steer (front)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `bump_steer_shims_front`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Sets how **front toe changes through travel** — the toe-link angle decides whether a wheel
gains toe-in or toe-out as it compresses (and the reverse on extension); shims change that angle. It's
[[toe-and-scrub]] made dynamic: the loaded (compressed) front runs a different toe than its static
value. Shim count isn't a fixed number — measure toe at ride height vs full compressi

chunks.title: bump-steer-toe-gain — Toe gain (rear)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `toe_gain_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]]

**Physics.** The rear version of the same mechanism: the toe-link angle sets how **rear toe changes
through travel**, so the loaded (compressed) outer rear runs a different toe than static. Shims set the
curve, not the static toe. What separates gained toe from static rear toe is **when it exists**: static
toe is always there; gained toe-in appears only as the wheel compresses — under roll, and as the rear

chunks.title: camber — Camber
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `camber_front`, `camber_rear`
**Concepts:** [[camber-grip]], [[camber-gain]]

**Physics.** Camber is the **tilt** of the tyre relative to the road. More **negative** camber tilts the
top of the tyre inward, helping the **outside** tyre stay nearer flat as the car rolls. The tyre runs
its **static** camber plus [[camber-gain]] in roll; what that effective tilt does to grip is [[camber-grip]].

chunks.title: caster — Front caster
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `caster_front`
**Concepts:** [[camber-grip]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Front caster tilts the **steering axis** back, so the contact patch trails behind where that
axis meets the ground (**mechanical trail**). Two things follow as you steer: the front wheel **gains
camber** (leaning into the corner — feeds [[camber-grip]]), and cornering force acting on the trail
creates a **self-aligning torque** that centres the steering. Most of caster's effect shows up

chunks.title: caster — Rear caster
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `caster_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]]

**Physics.** Rear caster acts partly like a small **wheelbase** change (shifts the effective fore-aft
distance between the contact patches) and **interacts with rear toe through travel** — change it and the
rear toe-gain curve ([[toe-and-scrub]]) usually needs re-trimming to match.

chunks.title: damper-oil — Damper oil (thicker vs lighter)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `damper_oil_front`, `damper_oil_rear`
**Concepts:** [[damping]], [[bite-hold]], [[oil-viscosity-temperature]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** Thicker oil raises the **damping force** for a given shaft speed (pistons and holes shape
the curve); lighter lowers it. It's the main knob that sets how much [[damping]] you have.

chunks.title: diff-and-driveline — Differential (rear gear diff)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `diff_oil`
**Concepts:** [[differential-coupling]], [[oil-viscosity-temperature]]

**Physics.** Thicker diff oil raises the diff's **coupling** — it resists a speed difference between the
rear wheels more strongly; thinner frees it. (Ball-diff tightness, one-ways, and a spool are other ways
to set coupling on cars that use them.)

chunks.title: diff-and-driveline — Differential — rotation direction (on power vs off power)
chunks.excerpt:
**Sign (founder-confirmed 2026-07-31):** more coupling (thicker `diff_oil`) **restricts rotation off
throttle** and **increases rotation on throttle**. Thinner is the mirror.

**Off throttle** there is no drive torque to share, so the diff only resists the speed difference the
arc demands. More coupling pulls the rear wheels toward one speed, opposing the yaw the corner asks
for: the car turns in less and holds tighter through entry and a coasting mid-corner.

**On thr

chunks.title: diff-and-driveline — Front driveline (spool) — context, not a lever
chunks.excerpt:
Touring cars run a **spool** front: both front wheels locked to one speed, no coupling knob. It
interacts with steering because steering asks the front wheels for *different* speeds while the spool
forbids it — see steering-geometry-ackermann.

chunks.title: droop-downstop — Droop and downstop (extension travel)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `droop_front`, `droop_rear`, `downstop_front`, `downstop_rear`
**Concepts:** [[bump-compliance]], [[load-transfer]]

**Physics.** Droop/downstop set how far a wheel can **extend** before it hits its **limit**. More
extension lets the wheel reach down to keep **contact** over bumps and as the car rolls; run out of it
and the wheel **tops out** — it can't extend further, so from there that corner goes rigid in droop and
load transfers through a stiff path. Sheet

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Chassis flex (general + front/rear)
chunks.excerpt:
**Concepts:** [[chassis-flex]]

**Physics.** How much the chassis **twists and bends** under load — see [[chassis-flex]]. Front vs rear
flex biases which end is softened.

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Chassis material
chunks.excerpt:
**Key:** `chassis`
**Concepts:** [[chassis-flex]], [[load-transfer]]

**Physics.** The plate material/construction sets baseline **flex** ([[chassis-flex]]) and can also change
**CoG height** ([[load-transfer]]) — e.g. a denser steel plate sits mass lower than carbon. Match part
numbers to your manufacturer sheet.

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Top decks, brace screws, deck cuts
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `top_deck_front`, `top_deck_rear`, `top_deck_screws`, `motor_mount_screws`, `top_deck_cuts`
**Concepts:** [[chassis-flex]]

**Physics.** Local **flex** adjusters ([[chassis-flex]]): a wider/stiffer top deck, **more engaged
screws**, and **fewer cuts** each add stiffness in their zone; the reverse adds flex. Front-half adjusters
bias front flex, rear-half rear. The A–H grid and part names are kit-specific — use your sheet.

chunks.title: ride-height-and-rake — Ride height
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `ride_height_front`, `ride_height_rear`
**Concepts:** [[load-transfer]], [[roll-center]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** Ride height sets **CoG height**, scaling the **total** load transfer ([[load-transfer]]). It
also moves the **suspension geometry** — where the arms sit in travel, so the roll centres and static
camber shift ([[roll-center]]). Too low and the chassis **bottoms**: the platform goes solid and the tyre
unloads ([[bump-compliance]]). A one-en

chunks.title: ride-height-and-rake — Rake (front vs rear ride height)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `ride_height_front`, `ride_height_rear`
**Concepts:** [[load-transfer]], [[roll-center]]

**Physics.** Rake is the **front/rear ride-height difference** — it sets static **attitude** and where
each end's geometry sits in travel (front vs rear roll centres and CoG bias shift with it). A geometry +
weight-bias change at both ends at once.

chunks.title: servo-horn-steering-response — Servo horn height (steering response)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `servo_horn_height` — the length of the servo horn the steering linkage attaches to.

**It effectively changes the speed of the servo: a shorter servo horn is smoother** (founder-confirmed). Mechanism: the horn is the lever between servo rotation and steering-rack movement — a **shorter horn moves the rack less per degree of servo rotation**, so steering inputs arrive slower and finer-grained; a **taller horn** delivers more rack movement per degree — faster, more

chunks.title: shock-geometry
chunks.excerpt: This file covers the **linkage geometry between the wheel and the damper** — where the shock mounts, how far it leans, its length, and end-of-travel limiters. Different lever from the **spring** (its stiffness — **spring-rate.md**) and the **damper oil** (its fluid — **damper-oil.md**): the same spring and oil feel different at the wheel depending on this geometry. Platforms with a lever/pushrod damper (e.g. Awesomatix) reach these effects through **spring gap** and **damper

chunks.title: shock-geometry — Motion ratio — mounting position and angle
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `shock_angle_front`, `shock_angle_rear`, `shock_mount_arm_front`, `shock_mount_arm_rear`, `shock_position_front`, `shock_position_rear` — sheet labels vary (hole numbers on tower and arm); read the column.

**Physics.** The **motion ratio** is how far the shock compresses per unit of wheel travel. Two independent strands set it:

- **Lever — where the lower mount sits on the arm.** The mount moves with the arm, so shock travel scales with the mount's distance fr

chunks.title: shock-geometry — Bump stops, packing, and internal limiters
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `bump_stop_front`, `bump_stop_rear`, `shock_limiter_front`, `shock_limiter_rear` — spacers, foam, o-rings, or shims that halt or ramp compression near the **end of the stroke**.

**Physics.** Unlike the spring, a bump stop does nothing until the suspension is deep in compression, then adds a **steep rate rise** at the end of travel. It is the **progressive** relative of the **upstop** hard cap (`drafts/upstop-compression-travel.md`): both govern the compressed end

chunks.title: shock-geometry — Shock length and travel window
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `shock_length_front`, `shock_length_rear` — length plus internal limiters set the **available travel window** (extension = droop, compression = up-travel).

**Physics.** Shock length and internal limiters bound how far the wheel can extend and compress. Setting **droop via the shock** is the **same mechanism** as the droop/downstop in **droop-downstop.md**; up-travel limiting overlaps with **bump stops** and **upstop** above. The shock hardware is simply *one way*

chunks.title: spring-rate — Spring rate
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `spring_front`, `spring_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-stiffness]], [[bite-hold]], [[motion-ratio]], [[tyre-load-sensitivity]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** A higher spring rate resists both **heave** (both wheels together) and **roll** more at
that end, and lets that end take load **faster** (it rolls less, so load arrives sooner).

chunks.title: steering-geometry-ackermann — Ackermann (steering-link position)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `inner_steering_angle`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** In a corner the **inside** front runs a **tighter** radius, so it needs **more** steering
angle. Ackermann sets how inner vs outer angles develop as you steer: **more ackermann** points each
front closer to its own arc; **less** (toward parallel) makes them take up more similar angles, loading
the pair harder — [[toe-and-scrub]] across steering, not travel.

chunks.title: steering-geometry-ackermann — Steering throw
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `steer_travel_out`
**Concepts:** [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Caps the **maximum** steering angle — more throw = tighter minimum radius but coarser
proportional control. It doesn't change the ackermann relationship, only how much of it you can reach.

chunks.title: toe — Toe (front & rear)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `toe_front`, `toe_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Sets the **static** toe at each end — how far the wheels point in or out at ride height.
Touring fronts are often run **toe-out**, rears **toe-in**; what toe does to the tyre is [[toe-and-scrub]].
Sheet signs differ — confirm whether a bigger number means more toe-in or toe-out before comparing.

chunks.title: under-hub — Under-hub shims (axle height / outer lower)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `under_hub_shims_front`, `under_hub_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]]

**Physics.** Adding shims under the hub pushes the **outer** end of the lower arm down — further from
the hub — flattening the lower arm, which **raises the roll centre** on that corner. Removing shims
does the reverse. A pure RC move — it adds nothing beyond roll centre.

**Effects (context-dependent — confirm on track).**
- All of them are that roll-centre change working through

chunks.title: under-lower-arm — Under-lower-arm shims (inner lower pickup)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `under_lower_arm_shims_ff`, `under_lower_arm_shims_fr`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rf`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rr`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]]

**Physics.** Adding shims under the inner end of the lower arm raises that pickup, tilting the lower
arm — which **raises the roll centre** on that corner. It is the **strongest single lever on roll
centre** (far more RC per shim than the upper link or the hub), and it moves RC and camber gain
together in the same direct

chunks.title: upper-link-geometry — Upper-link geometry (inner + outer shims)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `upper_inner_shims_ff`, `upper_inner_shims_fr`, `upper_inner_shims_rf`, `upper_inner_shims_rr`, `upper_outer_shims_front`, `upper_outer_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]], [[camber-gain]]

**Physics.** The upper link's angle relative to the lower arm (viewed from the front of the car) sets
roll centre and camber gain on that corner. The signs below are stated per key — read them there, not
from the angle.

Moving **both ends the same amount** (parallel

chunks.title: upper-link-geometry — Roll-centre direction per key (solver-checked, Awesomatix A800)
chunks.excerpt:
Read the sign here. Do not derive it from whether the link looks "flatter" or "more angled" — that
framing requires already knowing which end of the link sits higher, and it is exactly where the
direction gets inverted.

**Adding** shims (per 0.5 mm; front and rear behave the same):
- `upper_inner_shims_*` → **RC DOWN** (~0.5 mm), **less** camber gain
- `upper_outer_shims_*` → **RC UP** (~0.5 mm), **more** camber gain
- `under_lower_arm_shims_*` → **RC UP** (~1.1 mm),

chunks.title: weight-distribution-and-ballast — Static weight distribution (front %)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `weight_balance_front_percent`, `total_weight`
**Concepts:** [[load-transfer]], [[tyre-load-sensitivity]], [[polar-moment]]

**Physics.** Sets the **front/rear share** of the car's weight — the static load each axle carries before
transfer ([[load-transfer]]). Grip rises **less than proportionally** with load ([[tyre-load-sensitivity]]),
so moving the split changes how well each end converts its load; shifting mass fore/aft also moves the
[[polar-moment]].

chunks.title: weight-distribution-and-ballast — Ballast placement
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `motor_lateral_shift`
**Concepts:** [[load-transfer]], [[polar-moment]]

**Physics.** Rules set a minimum weight; ballast is where you place the rest. **Height** sets **CoG**,
scaling the **total** load transfer ([[load-transfer]]); **distance from centre** (fore/aft or lateral)
sets the [[polar-moment]]; **left/right** trims lateral balance. Moving a battery or motor shifts several
at once — re-scale after.

chunks.title: aero-load — Aerodynamic load
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The bodyshell (and any wing) makes an **aerodynamic vertical load** as air flows over it,
and that force grows with the **square of speed**: double the speed, roughly **four times** the load. So
it adds real grip in **fast** sections and **almost nothing** slow. Where it acts — more front or rear —
biases grip at speed; and because it scales with speed², that **balance itself shifts with speed**.

**Moved by:** bodyshell height / position, body choice.

chunks.title: bite-hold — Bite vs hold
chunks.excerpt:
*(driver-facing terms for what's canonically "initial vs overall grip"; the Engineer usually says
"bite / hold")*

**Feel — not physics.** Think of a grip curve: across the bottom is *how hard you're asking the
tyre* (how much you're leaning on it), up the side is grip.
- **Bite** (initial grip): the curve peaks **sooner, higher, and narrower**. Grip shows up fast and
  the ceiling is high — but the peak is a spike, and once you ask past it grip **drops away sharply**.

chunks.title: bite-hold — Feel vocabulary (the closed list)
chunks.excerpt:
These are the **only** words available for describing how a change feels. The list is closed:
anything outside it is not a feel word that needs replacing with a better adjective, it is a sign
the change has not been understood well enough to predict its feel — in which case say what the
change does **mechanically**, or name **where in the corner** and **what the car does there**, and
stop.

- **Grip arriving:** `bite`, `initial grip`, `overall grip`, `hold`
- **Bite en

chunks.title: bump-compliance — Bump compliance
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre grips most consistently when the **vertical load** pressing it into the road stays
**steady**. A rough or bumpy surface throws that load up and down. The suspension can **absorb** those
inputs — the wheel moves, less reaches the chassis, the load stays steadier — or **pass them through**,
so the load spikes and drops and the tyre can skip or briefly go **light** (no load, no grip). How much
it absorbs is set by how freely the wheel can move for a road

chunks.title: camber-gain — Camber gain (camber in roll)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Camber gain is how much **negative camber a wheel gains as its suspension compresses**.
As the car leans, the linkage adds negative camber to the compressing wheel, working against the lean
— how much is pure geometry. Static camber (`camber_front` / `camber_rear`) sets only the starting
angle, not the gain.

**Roll is what calls on it.** How far each wheel swings from static scales with how much the car
**rolls** ([[roll-stiffness]]); gain decides how much

chunks.title: camber-grip — Camber and grip
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre makes its best **lateral grip** at a certain **effective camber** (its static camber
plus [[camber-gain]] in roll) — enough tilt to keep the loaded contact patch working, not so much that
the patch shrinks. More camber builds peak lateral grip **up to that optimum**, then grip **falls off**,
often sharply; less camber gives a **lower peak** but a **more progressive** slip. A cambered tyre also
makes a little lateral force on its own (**camber thrust**)

chunks.title: chassis-flex — Chassis flex
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The chassis itself **twists and bends** under cornering and one-wheel (diagonal) loads —
it's a **spring in series with the suspension's roll stiffness** ([[roll-stiffness]]). The more it
flexes, the more of the roll it takes up itself, **softening the effective roll stiffness** and blurring
how cleanly the front/rear split tunes; it also adds **compliance** ([[bump-compliance]]) — the whole
platform gives over bumps and uneven surfaces. Front vs rear flex bi

chunks.title: corner-regime — Corner regime (steady-state vs transient)
chunks.excerpt:
**Concepts:** [[bite-hold]], [[roll-stiffness]], [[tyre-load-sensitivity]]

**Physics.** Stiffness changes act through two mechanisms that dominate in different kinds of
corner. Which one governs depends on whether the car reaches **steady state** — a constant roll
angle held under constant speed and radius — before the corner is over.

A corner is steady-state when both hold:

- **Enough time.** The chassis takes a roughly fixed time (a property of springs, dampers,

chunks.title: damping — Damping
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A damper resists movement with a force that grows the **faster the suspension moves** —
near nothing at rest, more on a quick input or bump. So it doesn't set *where* the car sits (springs
do) — it sets **how fast** the car gets there: how quickly it rolls and pitches, and how sharply it
reacts to inputs and bumps. More damping → slower, more controlled movement; less → faster, more
reactive. Because it acts on rate, it governs the **speed of the elastic (spr

chunks.title: differential-coupling — Differential coupling
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A differential lets the two **driven** wheels turn at **different speeds** — which they
must through a corner, since the outer wheel travels further. **Coupling** is how strongly the diff
**resists** that speed difference: **free** (open) at one extreme, fully **locked** (a spool — both
wheels forced to one speed) at the other. On power, more coupling drives the two wheels **more
together**, forcing the loaded outer and lighter inner toward the same speed aga

chunks.title: friction-circle — Friction circle (one grip budget, shared)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre has **one** grip budget at any instant, and cornering and driving/braking both
spend it. Grip used lengthways — putting power down, slowing the car — is grip that is no longer
available sideways, and the reverse. A tyre already at its limit sideways has nothing left for
throttle; a tyre spending everything on drive has nothing left to hold a line.

So the same tyre that grips fine at steady throttle can let go when drive force is added at the same
le

chunks.title: load-transfer — Load transfer
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Under cornering, braking or power, vertical load shifts across the tyres — **laterally**
(inside → outside in a corner) and **fore-aft** (rear → front under brakes, front → rear on power). The
**total** is set by **CoG height** with **track width** (lateral) or **wheelbase** (fore-aft) and the g;
most knobs only change *how fast* and *where* it moves — a few move the total: track width, and anything
that changes **CoG** (ride height, ballast, chassis).

Two

chunks.title: motion-ratio — Motion ratio
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The ratio between how far the **wheel** moves and how far the **spring/damper** moves —
set by where the unit mounts on the arm. A unit mounted further inboard moves less than the wheel, so
its **effective rate at the wheel is lower** than its nominal rate. Motion ratio scales **both**
effective spring rate and effective damping — the same spring or oil gives a different wheel rate as
the mounting changes, and it can vary through the travel.

**Moved by:**

chunks.title: oil-viscosity-temperature — Oil viscosity vs temperature
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Oil thins as it heats and thickens as it cools — lower viscosity hot, higher
viscosity cold. So the same nominal oil gives **more damping when cold** (early in a run, cold
track) and **less as it warms**. A property of the fluid, independent of car or setup.

**Affects:** damper oil [[damper-oil]] (`damper_oil_front`, `damper_oil_rear`), diff oil
[[diff-and-driveline]], any silicone fluid.

chunks.title: on-in-track — On the track vs in the track
chunks.excerpt:
*(a subjective feel that refers directly to roll-centre height)*

**Feel — not physics.** Where the car carries itself, set by how high or low the roll centre is:
- **On the track** (higher RC): the car sits **up on** the surface — reactive, quick to roll, lively,
  and nervous if your inputs aren't smooth; you drive a little *within* the car.
- **In the track** (lower RC): the car sits **down in** the surface — planted, smoother, safer, easy to
  lean on with throttle.

chunks.title: polar-moment — Polar moment (yaw inertia)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Polar moment is the car's resistance to **yaw** — rotating about its vertical axis. It's
set by **how far the mass sits from the centre**: mass gathered **near the CoG** gives a **low** polar
moment, mass out **toward the ends** a **high** one. For a given yaw effort, how fast the car starts —
and stops — rotating goes **inversely** with it: low → **quick, eager** direction changes; high →
**steadier, lazier** yaw that resists being turned and resists being s

chunks.title: roll-center — Roll centre
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The roll centre (RC) is the geometric point the sprung mass rolls about in a corner,
set by the suspension-linkage pickup points (arm and link angles). Its **height** sets four things:
- **How much load transfers the fast, geometric way** — the higher the RC, the larger the fraction of
  lateral load that reaches the outside tyres through the links (near-instant) rather than through the
  springs (slow). It sets the fast fraction in [[load-transfer]].
- **Ho

chunks.title: roll-stiffness — Roll stiffness (elastic)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** How strongly the car resists **body roll** through its **springs and anti-roll bars** —
the elastic path, as opposed to the geometry (that's [[roll-center]]). Springs resist both **heave**
(both wheels moving up together) and roll; an **ARB resists roll only** — it does nothing when both
wheels move together. It sets two things:

chunks.title: toe-and-scrub — Toe and scrub
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Toe is how far a wheel points **in** (toe-in) or **out** (toe-out) of dead-ahead. A toed
wheel already runs a small **slip angle** going straight, so it makes a bit of side force before you
even steer — with **toe-in** the two wheels' forces point **toward** each other, with **toe-out**
**apart**; they cancel going straight but pre-load how the pair takes a set. That constant slip also

chunks.title: tyre-load-sensitivity — Tyre load sensitivity
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre makes more grip the more vertical load it carries — but **less than
proportionally**: double the load and you get less than double the grip; grip-per-unit-load falls as
load rises. So loading one tyre of a pair much harder than the other makes **less grip from the pair**
than sharing the load evenly would, all else equal.

A property of the tyre itself.
